introduction: Today we begin Advent and a new liturgical year, the year of Saint Matthew's Gospel. Isaiah sees all nations streaming to the mountain of the Lord, where swords are beaten into plowshares. Paul tells us that the night is almost over and the day is near. Jesus urges us to stay awake, for the Son of Man will come at an hour we do not expect. Let us begin this season watchful and full of hope.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, our salvation is nearer now than when we first believed. Let us bring our prayers to the Lord who is coming.
intentions: For the Church as she begins a new liturgical year: that she may wait for Christ with watchful and joyful hearts. Let us pray to the Lord.
For peace among nations: that weapons of war may be turned into tools for feeding the hungry. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who live in darkness or despair: that the light of Christ may dawn for them. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are too busy or distracted to think of God: that this Advent may wake them up. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may cast off the works of darkness and put on the Lord Jesus Christ. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, at the beginning of Advent, help us to wake from sleep and walk in your light, so that we may be ready to welcome your Son when he comes. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Stay awake
reflection.body:
A new liturgical year begins today. This year, most Sunday Gospels will come from Saint Matthew, who shows us Jesus as the teacher and the fulfillment of God's promises to Israel.

Advent opens with a great vision. Isaiah sees "the mountain of the LORD's house" raised above every hill, and "all nations shall flow to it." People will say, "Come, let's go up to the mountain of the LORD... and he will teach us of his ways." And the result will be peace: "They shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks." This is the future God promises, and Isaiah invites us to start living it now: "come, and let's walk in the light of the LORD."

Paul sounds an alarm: "it is already time for you to awaken out of sleep, for salvation is now nearer to us than when we first believed." He uses the image of dawn: "The night is far gone, and the day is near." So he tells us to "throw off the deeds of darkness" and "put on the Lord Jesus Christ."

In the Gospel, Jesus compares the coming of the Son of Man to the days of Noah. People were "eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage," living ordinary lives without any thought of God, and the flood took them by surprise. Two people will be working side by side; one will be taken, the other left. The difference is not what they are doing but whether they are ready. "Watch therefore, for you don't know in what hour your Lord comes."

Advent is a wake-up call. This week, light the first candle of an Advent wreath at home and pray each evening. Ask yourself: what deeds of darkness do I need to throw off? And put on Christ in one concrete act of love.
